items.prompt: What is the hard, outer covering of a tooth called?

options.label: Dentin
options.feedback: Dentin is the layer beneath the enamel, not the outer covering. It is softer than enamel and makes up most of the tooth's body.

options.label: Enamel
options.feedback: Correct. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body and forms the protective outer layer of the crown of each tooth.

options.label: Pulp
options.feedback: Pulp is the soft inner tissue containing nerves and blood vessels, not the outer covering. It sits at the center of the tooth.

options.label: Cementum
options.feedback: Cementum covers the root below the gum line, not the crown. The outer covering of the visible part of the tooth is enamel.

items.ok_line: Enamel is the hard outer shell of a tooth.
items.ko_line: Remember the layers: enamel outside, dentin, then pulp.
items.exp_text: Enamel is the hard, mineral-rich outer layer of the crown, the part you see. It protects the softer dentin and pulp underneath from wear and damage.

items.prompt: Which type of tooth is mainly used for tearing food apart?

options.label: Incisor
options.feedback: Incisors are flat-edged teeth used for cutting or biting off food, not tearing. Tearing is done by pointed teeth.

options.label: Premolar
options.feedback: Premolars have a flatter surface with ridges and help crush and grind food, not tear it. They sit between canines and molars.

options.label: Molar
options.feedback: Molars are broad and bumpy for grinding food into smaller pieces, not for tearing. They are at the back of the mouth.

options.label: Canine
options.feedback: Correct. Canines are pointed and cone-shaped, designed to grip and tear food like meat.

items.ok_line: Canines are the pointed tearing teeth.
items.ko_line: Think of the shape: pointed means tearing, flat means cutting, bumpy means grinding.
items.exp_text: Canine teeth have a single sharp point, which lets them pierce and tear food. They are particularly useful for eating meat.

items.prompt: What is the soft tissue inside a tooth that contains nerves and blood vessels?

options.label: Enamel
options.feedback: Enamel is the hard outer layer with no nerves or blood vessels. The soft inner tissue is what you are looking for.

options.label: Dentin
options.feedback: Dentin is a hard, calcified tissue under enamel, but it is not soft and does not contain nerves. The pulp is the soft inner part.

options.label: Pulp
options.feedback: Correct. The pulp is the central soft area of a tooth containing nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue.

options.label: Cementum
options.feedback: Cementum is a hard layer covering the root, not soft tissue. It helps anchor the tooth in the jawbone.

items.ok_line: The pulp holds nerves and blood vessels.
items.ko_line: Only pulp is soft and living inside the tooth.
items.exp_text: The pulp is the innermost part of the tooth, a soft tissue that supplies nutrients and sensation. It extends down into the root through narrow canals.

items.prompt: How many sets of teeth does a person typically grow in a lifetime?

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Correct. Humans grow a first set of baby teeth (milk teeth) and then a permanent set of adult teeth.

options.label: One
options.feedback: Only one set would mean no milk teeth, but children have a first set that falls out. Adults get a second set.

options.label: Three
options.feedback: There are not three sets. The permanent set is the last one; wisdom teeth are part of that same set, not a separate one.

options.label: Four
options.feedback: No, there are only two sets in a typical human lifetime: the deciduous (baby) set and the permanent set.

items.ko_line: Remember: a first set, then a second permanent set.
items.exp_text: The first set, called milk teeth or baby teeth, appears in childhood and is eventually replaced. The second and final set is permanent and lasts into adulthood.

items.prompt: Which tooth layer is the hardest substance in the human body?

options.label: Dentin
options.feedback: Dentin is hard but not as hard as enamel. It is the layer under the enamel and is more yellowish.

options.label: Pulp
options.feedback: Pulp is soft tissue, not hard at all. The hardest substance is a mineral-based outer layer.

options.label: Cementum
options.feedback: Cementum is hard but softer than enamel. It covers the root and is not the hardest tissue in the body.

options.label: Enamel
options.feedback: Correct. Enamel is composed mainly of minerals and is the hardest substance in the human body, even harder than bone.

items.ko_line: Only enamel is the hardest; dentin and cementum are softer.
items.exp_text: Enamel is almost entirely made of minerals, especially hydroxyapatite, giving it extreme hardness to withstand chewing forces without wearing away quickly.

items.prompt: What is the visible part of a tooth that sits above the gum line called?

options.label: Root
options.feedback: The root is below the gum line, anchoring the tooth in the jawbone. The visible part is above the gums.

options.label: Crown
options.feedback: Correct. The crown is the part of the tooth that is visible in the mouth, covered by enamel.

options.label: Neck
options.feedback: The neck is the narrow area where the crown meets the root, at the gum line, not the whole visible part.

options.label: Pulp
options.feedback: Pulp is the inner soft tissue, not a visible part of the tooth's structure from outside.

items.ok_line: The crown is above the gums.
items.ko_line: Think of the crown as the top you can see.
items.exp_text: The crown is the portion of the tooth that emerges from the gum and is used for biting and chewing. It is completely covered by enamel.

items.prompt: What is the role of the root of a tooth?

options.label: To chew food
options.feedback: Chewing is done by the crown, not the root. The root is hidden below the gum line.

options.label: To sense temperature
options.feedback: Temperature sensing happens in the pulp, not the root itself. The root's main job is anchoring.

options.label: To anchor the tooth in the jawbone
options.feedback: Correct. The root extends into the jawbone and holds the tooth firmly in place.

options.label: To protect the crown
options.feedback: The crown is protected by enamel, not the root. The root is below the gums and doesn't cover the crown.

items.ok_line: The root holds the tooth firmly.
items.ko_line: The root is for support, not for chewing or sensing.
items.exp_text: The root is embedded in the jawbone and covered by cementum. It keeps the tooth stable during chewing and prevents it from falling out.

items.prompt: Which teeth are the last molars at the back of the mouth that often erupt in the late teens or early twenties?

options.label: Wisdom teeth
options.feedback: Correct. Wisdom teeth are the third molars that typically appear between ages 17 and 25.

options.label: Incisors
options.feedback: Incisors are the front teeth, not at the back. They erupt much earlier in childhood.

options.label: Canines
options.feedback: Canines are pointed teeth near the front, not last molars. They come in well before the late teens.

options.label: Premolars
options.feedback: Premolars sit between canines and molars, and they erupt before the last molars. They are not the final set of teeth.

items.ok_line: Wisdom teeth are the final molars.
items.ko_line: Only the third molars are called wisdom teeth.
items.exp_text: Wisdom teeth are the third set of molars, located at the very back. They often cause issues because the jaw may not have enough room for them.

items.prompt: What is the first set of teeth that children grow called?

options.label: Permanent teeth
options.feedback: Permanent teeth are the second set that replace the first set. The first set is different and temporary.

options.label: Adult teeth
options.feedback: Adult teeth is another name for the permanent set, not the first set that children have.

options.label: Milk teeth
options.feedback: Correct. Milk teeth, also called baby teeth or deciduous teeth, are the first set that children have.

options.label: Wisdom teeth
options.feedback: Wisdom teeth are a type of permanent molar, not the first set. They appear much later.

items.ok_line: Milk teeth are the first set.
items.ko_line: The first set is temporary, called milk teeth.
items.exp_text: Milk teeth, also known as baby teeth, start appearing in infancy and are eventually replaced by permanent teeth as the jaw grows.

items.prompt: What is the process of tooth decay that creates a hole in the tooth called?

options.label: Plaque
options.feedback: Plaque is the sticky film of bacteria on teeth, not the hole itself. The hole is the result of decay.

options.label: Cavity
options.feedback: Correct. A cavity is a hole in the tooth caused by acids from bacteria that break down enamel and dentin.

options.label: Erosion
options.feedback: Erosion is the wearing away of enamel by acids, but a cavity specifically refers to the hole formed by decay.

options.label: Gingivitis
options.feedback: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums, not a hole in the tooth. It affects soft tissue, not the tooth itself.

items.ok_line: A cavity is a decayed hole.
items.ko_line: Cavity is the correct term for the hole.
items.exp_text: Cavities form when bacteria in plaque produce acids that dissolve tooth enamel, eventually creating a hole. If untreated, they can reach the pulp and cause pain.
